paragraphs.heading: A script of many kinds of sign
paragraphs.text: Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal script ancient Egyptians used to write their own language. The system mixed several kinds of sign: some stood for ideas or whole words, some for syllables, and some for single sounds, much like letters. Altogether it had more than 1,000 different characters. Scholars sort the glyphs into three groups. Phonetic signs record sounds, and some of them each stand for one consonant, working like an alphabet; logographs stand for units of meaning; and determinatives are added to narrow down what a written word means.

paragraphs.heading: Where the signs came from
paragraphs.text: Hieroglyphs may have grown out of Egypt's older artistic traditions. Symbols on Gerzean pottery from around 4000 BC have been argued to look like hieroglyphic writing. Simpler symbol systems, called proto-writing, appeared in the second half of the 4th millennium BC. Examples include clay labels of a ruler known as Scorpion I, found at Abydos in 1998, and the Narmer Palette. The oldest full sentence in mature hieroglyphs found so far is on a seal impression from the tomb of Seth-Peribsen, from the Second Dynasty in the 28th or 27th century BC.

paragraphs.heading: Invented at home or borrowed
paragraphs.text: Scholars have long argued over whether Egyptians invented writing on their own or took it from cuneiform, the script developed to write Sumerian in southern Mesopotamia. Some, such as Geoffrey Sampson, held that Egyptian writing appeared a little after the Sumerian script and was probably shaped by it. Yet there is no direct evidence of writing passing from one land to the other, so the question has not been settled. Glyphs from Abydos dated to between 3400 and 3200 BC cast further doubt on the old view that the Mesopotamian signs came first. Hieroglyphs are now thought to be one of four writing systems that arose without outside influence, along with cuneiform, Chinese characters and Mayan script.

paragraphs.heading: Everyday scripts and monuments
paragraphs.text: In the Middle Kingdom the system matured into a script for monumental inscriptions, using about 900 different signs. As writing spread among Egyptians, simpler forms of the signs developed into hieratic, the priestly script, and demotic, the popular one. Both suited writing on papyrus better than hieroglyphs did. A cursive form of hieroglyph was also used for religious texts on papyrus and wood. Hieroglyphs were not pushed aside, though; they lived on next to the newer scripts, above all in monuments and formal writing. The Rosetta Stone carries writing in three parallel scripts: hieroglyphs, demotic and the Greek alphabet.

paragraphs.heading: Fading from use
paragraphs.text: Hieroglyphs stayed in use through the New Kingdom and beyond, under Persian rule and then in the Ptolemaic and Roman periods that followed Alexander the Great's conquest of Egypt. Greek and Roman writers, having learned the signs were sacred, pictured this complex but rational system as a magical code carrying secret, mystical knowledge. By the 4th century AD few Egyptians could still read them, and late uses reach into that century. When pagan temples throughout Roman Egypt were shut for good in the 5th century, it meant that fluent readers and writers, called scribes, were lost. The script's nature stayed unknown through the Middle Ages until Jean-François Champollion deciphered it in the 1820s, helped by the Rosetta Stone.

paragraphs.heading: Ancestor of many alphabets
paragraphs.text: Hieroglyphs also gave rise to the Proto-Sinaitic script, which later became the Phoenician alphabet, the first phonetic writing system to be widely adopted. Phoenician in turn led to the Greek and Aramaic scripts. Through Greek came Latin and Cyrillic, and through Aramaic came Arabic and the Brahmic scripts. As a result, most of the world's living writing systems trace their family line back to Egyptian hieroglyphs.
